conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in with abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me what’s been going on at home since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It just didn’t get better. I’ve been taking the vancomycin like they told me, but I’m still having diarrhea a lot and I can’t keep food down. I feel dried out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How many times a day are you having diarrhea, roughly? And when was the last time you vomited?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was a lot at home—like all day. I threw up multiple times today before coming in. It’s mostly dry heaving now, but it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, blood in the stool, chest pain, shortness of breath, or burning when you pee?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. No blood. No breathing issues. Peeing is just not much because I’m not drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with dehydration. In the emergency department your vital signs were stable, and your blood work didn’t show a high white count. We’re giving you IV fluids now and medication for nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s the C. diff again. Why isn’t the antibiotic working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could still be related, but there are a couple possibilities: sometimes symptoms lag behind even when the infection is improving, and sometimes vomiting makes it hard to keep the medicine down. We’re going to re-test your stool for C. diff toxin/PCR and also check for other infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to do another scan? I’ve had so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A CT of your abdomen and pelvis was done tonight to make sure there’s no obstruction or severe colitis. The initial read shows no acute process—no dangerous swelling of the colon and no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With repeated vomiting and frequent diarrhea, the intestines can be very irritated, and dehydration can make pain feel worse. We’ll treat symptoms while we rule out anything dangerous. We’ll also keep your stomach-protecting medicines going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have that feeding tube history and the bypass reversal—could something be wrong with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your surgical history, we always take that seriously. The CT didn’t show a surgical complication or bowel obstruction. We’ll keep monitoring your belly exam closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something stronger for nausea? The Zofran helps a little but not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s schedule anti-nausea medication and keep it available as needed. The goal is to stop the vomiting so you can keep down fluids and your vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds? I don’t want to be judged, but it’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll treat your pain while keeping you safe. We’ll use acetaminophen and your home gabapentin, and we can use a small amount of opioid if needed, especially while you’re unable to eat and drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to stop feeling like I’m going to pass out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: your lactate is normal, which is reassuring, and your kidney function looks okay. We’ll continue IV fluids overnight and recheck labs in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I’m not septic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—right now there’s no sign of sepsis. We’re still taking cultures and stool tests, but nothing suggests a dangerous infection in your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing told me you were able to keep down a few sips of water. How’s the nausea at this moment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. My mouth feels less dry. Still crampy though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep the fluids running and aim to transition you to drinking on your own as soon as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Any vomiting since you got to the floor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. Still diarrhea, but not as constant as at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We sent stool testing for C. diff and also cultures for bacteria and parasites. While we wait, we’re continuing your oral vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the C. diff test comes back negative, why keep taking vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you were already on a planned taper for a recent recurrence. A negative test today suggests the infection may be clearing, but stopping abruptly can increase the risk of relapse. The plan is to continue the taper you were prescribed and have GI help decide when it’s safe to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the diarrhea could be from something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—diarrhea can persist from irritation after infection, from medications, or from other causes. The CT didn’t show anything acute, and your labs are reassuring, so we’re focusing on hydration, symptom control, and making sure there isn’t another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat? I’m afraid to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s start slowly—clear liquids first, then advance as tolerated. The key is small amounts frequently. If you feel nauseated, pause and use the antiemetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure always runs low. Are you worried about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now it’s on the low side but you’re not dizzy and your heart rate is okay. Dehydration can lower it. We’re also watching your propranolol because it can push blood pressure down further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did lunch go? Any vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept down some broth and crackers. Pain is still there but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep IV fluids for now and reassess later today—if you keep drinking, we can start turning them down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will the C. diff result be back? I’m anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should result this evening. I’ll check and let you know as soon as it’s posted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff PCR came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Negative? Then why am I still having diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A negative PCR means we didn’t detect toxigenic C. diff in the sample. The diarrhea can still take time to settle as your gut recovers, and dehydration itself can make you feel awful. The good news is we’re not seeing signs of severe colitis or another acute abdominal problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can stop the vancomycin now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Because you were treated for a recurrence recently, the safest plan is to continue the taper schedule you were already given and follow up with GI to decide the endpoint. Stopping suddenly can lead to symptoms flaring again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to be on antibiotics forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. The taper is designed to gradually reduce it. GI will reassess with you at follow-up and decide if any changes are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today compared with when you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’m not throwing up. Diarrhea is still there but way less. I’m tired though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what we’re seeing. Your exam is improved and you’re walking in the hallway. Your labs show some mild electrolyte changes and mild anemia compared to admission, which can happen with lots of fluids and illness—we’ll keep an eye on it, but nothing suggests bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the other stool tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far, stool cultures are negative for common bacteria like Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter, and the parasite tests don’t show ova and parasites or Giardia/Cryptosporidium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s basically just my gut being angry and me being dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading explanation given the negative infectious workup and the normal CT. The main treatment is hydration, continuing the planned vancomycin taper, and symptom control while your intestines recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure was low again this morning. Are you going to change my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Because your blood pressure has been low and you’re not having symptoms that require it urgently, we’re going to hold your propranolol for now and have you discuss restarting it with your outpatient doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous to stop it suddenly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At your dose, holding it is generally safe, especially since low blood pressure is the bigger immediate issue. If you notice palpitations, chest pain, or severe anxiety symptoms after stopping, you should call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep tolerating food and fluids today without vomiting, we can likely discharge you home later this afternoon. How does that sound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to go home, but I’m worried it’ll come right back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That worry makes sense given how many times you’ve been through this. The things that make us comfortable discharging are: you’re keeping down oral intake, your pain is controlled with oral meds, your vitals are stable, and the dangerous causes have been ruled out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I do if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the ondansetron as prescribed, take small sips of fluids, and if you can’t keep anything down or you feel faint, come back for care. Also come in for severe worsening abdominal pain, fever, or blood in stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get pain medicine to go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a small supply of oxycodone for moderate pain, and you can use acetaminophen for mild pain. Because opioids can worsen constipation and sometimes nausea, we want you to use the lowest amount needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I have diarrhea—why would constipation matter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bowel pattern can swing as you recover, especially once diarrhea improves. We’re keeping your bowel regimen medications as ‘as needed’ only, and you should avoid taking them unless you become constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s review your vancomycin plan: continue it exactly as the taper schedule from your last discharge. GI will see you in follow-up and help decide when to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you write it down? I get confused with the taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—we’ll put the step-by-step schedule in your discharge paperwork, and the pharmacy label will match it. If anything doesn’t match what you were told previously, call us or your GI office before changing doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds—my seizure medicine and my antidepressants?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your levetiracetam for seizures and your psychiatric medications as you were taking them. We’re also continuing your stomach protection medicines—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate—since you have a history of ulcers and reflux symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: you’ve had no vomiting here, your diarrhea is much less frequent, and you’re tolerating oral intake. Your blood cultures haven’t grown anything so far, and the remaining stool tests are negative. We’ll discharge you home today with instructions and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m relieved the C. diff test was negative, but I’ll keep taking the vancomycin taper and call if things get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. Remember: don’t restart propranolol until you’ve discussed it with your outpatient doctor because of the low blood pressure here. We’ll include that clearly in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want a normal day without my stomach controlling everything.
